etymology: Imitative, the sound of a ray gun or an electric jolt, first popularized in science-fiction comics (the Buck Rogers strip, from 1929). As a verb, to zap — to kill or destroy with a sudden blast, then to hit, defeat, or jolt — is mid-twentieth century; the 1960s gave it countercultural flair (Robert Crumb’s Zap Comix, 1968), and the 1970s–80s added zap in the microwave and zapping channels with a remote. Zapped also means exhausted.
biblical_def: To zap is to hit something with a sudden blast — a ray gun in a comic book, a bug in an electric trap, leftovers in the microwave, an enemy in a video game. It is the sound of instant, effortless destruction, and the Boomer generation grew up imagining it on Saturday-morning cartoons. The Christian observation: Scripture records a moment when two disciples wanted to zap their enemies, and the Lord’s answer is one of the most important rebukes in the Gospels. A Samaritan village refused to receive Jesus, and "when his disciples James and John saw this, they said, Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did? But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man is not come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them" (Luk 9:54–56). The zapping instinct — wipe out the people who annoy or oppose us — is the opposite of the gospel. God’s judgment is real and will come as suddenly as lightning: "as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be" (Mat 24:27). But the reason it has not yet come is mercy: "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance" (2Pe 3:9). Our children play games in which enemies are zapped by the hundred. A father can enjoy the game with them and still teach Luk 9:56: the Son of man came to save.
webster_summary: Imitative comic-book word (1929; mid-20th-c. verb) for destroying with a sudden blast, later to microwave, to channel-surf, or to exhaust — the instinct James and John showed in Luk 9:54, which the Lord rebuked: "the Son of man is not come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them" (Luk 9:56).
webster_full: ZAP, v.t. (mid-20th c.; Boomer-era slang) 1. To destroy or kill with a sudden blast, as of a ray gun. 2. To strike or jolt suddenly. 3. To cook or heat in a microwave oven (1970s–). 4. To change channels with a remote control (1980s). interj. The sound of such a blast. Zapped, adj., exhausted.
Imitative; first popularized in science-fiction comic strips (Buck Rogers, 1929).
Decode for families: video games are built on the zap. Teach the verse that rebukes it.

Luk 9:55

corruption_summary: The zap imagines effortless, instant destruction of whatever annoys us; Christ rebuked that spirit in His own disciples and delays His sure judgment out of longsuffering mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: Comic books and cartoons taught a generation to imagine power as the ability to blast an enemy instantly and without cost. Video games have perfected it. There is nothing wrong with a child’s game of pretend, but the imagination it trains can leak into real life — the wish to zap the rival, the critic, the irritating neighbor, the other political party. James and John, the "sons of thunder," had that wish, and they even had a biblical precedent in Elijah. Jesus rebuked them anyway: "Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of" (Luk 9:55).

The gospel’s power is the opposite of the zap. It is slow, patient, and costly: the Lord bore the fire Himself rather than calling it down on others. The judgment will come, sudden as lightning (Mat 24:27); until then, God’s patience is salvation (2Pe 3:9). A Christian who has been spared the fire he deserved will be slow to call it down on anyone else.
roots_summary: Imitative zap (ray-gun sound) → 1929 Buck Rogers comics → mid-20th-c. verb (to blast) → 1968 Zap Comix → 1970s–80s microwave and remote-control senses.
roots_lines: Imitative English zap — the sound of a ray gun or electric shock
Mid-20th c.: to zap — to kill, destroy, or strike suddenly
usage: "Grandpa says when he was a kid, zap was the sound a ray gun made. Now it’s the sound his coffee makes in the microwave."
Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of (Luk 9:55).
The Son of man is not come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them (Luk 9:56).

etymology: From hack, to cut roughly (Old English haccian; Webster 1828: "to cut irregularly and into small pieces"), with the figurative sense of being cut up, irritated. Hacked off and hacked, meaning annoyed or angry, are mid-twentieth-century American slang, in common Boomer use by the 1960s–70s ("I was really hacked off about it"); compare ticked off and teed off. The British phrase hacked off, fed up, is similar.
biblical_def: To be hacked off is to be annoyed, irritated, angry — not quite furious, but definitely not happy. "Dad was hacked off about the dent in the car." The Christian observation: Scripture speaks to the everyday anger the slang names with more precision than we usually do. It does not say all anger is sin. "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath" (Eph 4:26). There is a righteous anger at evil. But most of what we call being hacked off is not righteous; it is wounded pride, frustrated plans, and impatience. James is plain: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:19–20). God put a question to the angry prophet Jonah that every hacked-off father should hear: "Doest thou well to be angry?" (Jon 4:4). Jonah was hacked off because God was merciful to his enemies and because a plant that shaded him died; God asked him to look at his anger honestly. Proverbs gives the way out: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" (Pro 15:1); and "The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression" (Pro 19:11). A father who is hacked off about a dented fender and chooses to pass over it, after the facts are known, is showing his son something of the patience of God.
webster_summary: Mid-20th-c. American slang (from hack, to cut roughly) for annoyed or angry — everyday anger Scripture permits only without sin (Eph 4:26), questions ("Doest thou well to be angry?" Jon 4:4), and answers with the glory of passing over a transgression (Pro 19:11).
webster_full: HACKED OFF, adj. (American slang, mid-20th c.; common Boomer use 1960s–70s) Annoyed, irritated, angry. Also hacked. Compare ticked off, teed off.
Webster (1828) — HACK, verb transitive 1. To cut irregularly and into small pieces; to notch; to mangle by repeated strokes of a cutting instrument.
Decode for families: name the anger, then ask Jonah’s question.
scriptures: Eph 4:26
Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:
Jas 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
Jon 4:4

Pro 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.

corruption_summary: The slang treats everyday anger as a normal mood to be announced; Scripture asks whether the anger is righteous, forbids nursing it, and commends the soft answer and the passing over of offenses.
corruption_paragraphs: Our language has dozens of mild words for anger — hacked off, ticked off, ticked, miffed, steamed — and their mildness can hide the seriousness of the thing. A man who is "just a little hacked off" all the time is a man whose household walks on eggshells. Scripture takes the low-grade, chronic irritability of a home seriously, because it poisons love slowly. Eph 4:26 sets a daily deadline: deal with it before sundown.

Jonah’s story is the best mirror. He was angry at God’s mercy and angry about his own comfort, and God answered him not with a lecture but with a question (Jon 4:4) and a lesson in compassion. The gospel answers our anger the same way: we who have been forgiven an enormous debt are asked to pass over the small ones (Pro 19:11).
roots_summary: Old English haccian (to cut in pieces) → hack (to cut roughly; 1828) → mid-20th-c. American slang hacked (off) (annoyed).
roots_lines: Old English haccian — to hack, to cut in pieces
English hack — to cut irregularly; to mangle by repeated strokes (1828)
1960s–70s: common in Boomer speech; compare ticked off, teed off
usage: "Grandpa got hacked off at the umpire, then apologized to him after the game. That’s the part I remember."
Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath (Eph 4:26).
Doest thou well to be angry? (Jon 4:4).

etymology: Catch in the sense of meeting up with someone ("I’ll catch you at lunch") + later. Catch you later — goodbye for now — is twentieth-century American colloquial, very common from the 1960s–70s, along with its clipped forms later, laters, and catch ya, and its CB-era cousin catch you on the flip side.
biblical_def: Catch you later is a casual goodbye that assumes a next time: "See you around; we’ll pick this up again." The Christian observation: every goodbye rests on an assumption Scripture asks us to say out loud. We assume there will be a later. James gently corrects the habit of talking as if tomorrow were ours: "Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city ... Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away. For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that" (Jas 4:13–15). "Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth" (Pro 27:1). The older generation’s farewell, "Lord willing," said exactly that. But Scripture also gives believers a later that is certain. At the graveside Paul comforts the church: "we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord. Wherefore comfort one another with these words" (1Th 4:17–18). For Christians, every goodbye — even the last one — is truly "catch you later." A grandmother who says it at the end of a phone call, and a grandson who says it at her bedside in the hospital, can both mean it with the full weight of the resurrection.
webster_summary: Mid-20th-c. American goodbye (common 1960s–70s; also later, catch you on the flip side) that assumes a next time — an assumption Scripture qualifies with "If the Lord will" (Jas 4:15) and fulfils for believers in the reunion of 1Th 4:17.
webster_full: CATCH YOU LATER, phr. (American colloquial, 20th c.; common Boomer use 1960s–70s) Goodbye; see you again. Also later, laters, catch ya; compare catch you on the flip side.
Webster (1828) — LATE, adverb 1. After the usual time, or the time appointed; after delay; as, he arrived late 2. After the proper or usual season. This year the fruits ripen late
Decode for families: add the old words, "Lord willing," and the phrase becomes a confession of faith.
scriptures: Jas 4:14
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
Jas 4:15
For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.
Pro 27:1
Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.
Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord.
Wherefore comfort one another with these words.
corruption_summary: A friendly goodbye that quietly presumes on tomorrow; Scripture teaches the believer to say "If the Lord will" and gives him a certain later in the resurrection.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong with catch you later. Its only weakness is the one James names: it speaks of tomorrow as if we owned it. Earlier generations of Christians wrote "D.V." — Deo volente, God willing — on their letters and plans. That habit was not superstition; it was humility, and it is worth reviving in our own speech.

The deeper comfort is that the Christian’s goodbyes are never final. Paul wrote 1Th 4:17–18 to grieving believers who wondered whether their dead were lost, and his answer was a reunion — "together with them" — in the presence of the Lord. Every Christian funeral is, in the end, a "catch you later."
roots_summary: Old North French cachier (to chase, to capture) → catch (to meet up with) + Old English læt (late) → 20th-c. American catch you later.
roots_lines: Old North French cachier — to chase, to hunt; English catch — to seize; to meet up with
1970s: catch you on the flip side (CB and radio slang)
usage: "Grandma always ends a call with ‘Catch you later, Lord willing.’ We used to laugh. Now we say it too."
Ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that (Jas 4:15).

etymology: Heads up! — look up, watch out — has been a shouted warning since at least the early twentieth century (on ships, building sites, and ball fields). The adjective heads-up, alert or clever ("heads-up play"), is mid-century sports slang; the noun a heads-up, advance notice or a warning ("Thanks for the heads-up"), spread in the 1970s–80s and is now standard workplace English.
biblical_def: Heads up! is a warning: look up, something is coming. A heads-up is advance notice: "Just giving you a heads-up — the meeting moved." The Christian observation: Scripture is full of heads-ups, and the people who give them are called watchmen. God told Ezekiel, "I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me" (Eze 33:7), and He laid a heavy responsibility on the watchman who saw danger and stayed silent: "if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned ... his blood will I require at the watchman’s hand" (Eze 33:6). The Lord Jesus gave His whole church a standing heads-up: "what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch" (Mar 13:37). Proverbs praises the man who heeds it: "A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished" (Pro 22:3). And there is a sweeter heads-up in the Gospel too: when the signs of the end appear, "then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh" (Luk 21:28). The Christian’s head is lifted not only in watchfulness but in hope, because the One coming is his Redeemer. David knew Him: "thou, O LORD, art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head" (Psa 3:3). A father is his family’s watchman. He gives heads-ups about danger — and he teaches his children to lift up their heads in hope.
webster_summary: A shouted warning (early 20th c.), then sports slang for alert play and, from the 1970s–80s, "advance notice" — the watchman’s duty of Eze 33:7, and the hopeful command, "look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh" (Luk 21:28).
webster_full: HEADS UP, interj. (early 20th c.–) Look out! Pay attention! HEADS-UP, n. (1970s–80s) Advance notice; a warning: "Thanks for the heads-up." adj. (sports, mid-20th c.) Alert, quick-witted: "a heads-up play."

Webster (1828) — HEAD, noun hed. 1. The uppermost part of the human body, or the foremost part of the body of prone and creeping animals. This part of the human body contains the organs of hearing, seeing, tasting and smelling; it contains also the brain, which is supposed to be the seat of the intellectual powers, and of sensation. Hence the head is the chief or more important part, and is used for the whole person, in the phrase, let the evil fall on my head
Decode for families: the best heads-up a parent gives is the one Ezekiel was told to give — early, clear, and from God’s Word.
scriptures: Eze 33:7
So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me.
Eze 33:6

But if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned; if the sword come, and take any person from among them, he is taken away in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at the watchman's hand.
And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.
Pro 22:3
A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.
And when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh.
Psa 3:3
But thou, O LORD, art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head.
corruption_summary: A useful, wholesome phrase; Scripture fills it with the watchman’s duty to warn and the believer’s privilege to lift up his head in hope of redemption.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in heads up. If anything, it rebukes a culture that has grown reluctant to warn. Parents hesitate to give their grown children a heads-up about a bad relationship or a dangerous habit; pastors hesitate to warn about sin; friends stay silent to avoid awkwardness. Ezekiel 33 says silence is not neutral: the watchman who sees the sword and says nothing shares the guilt.

Scripture’s heads-up has two tones. One is warning: watch, the danger is real (Mar 13:37). The other is hope: look up, your redemption is near (Luk 21:28). A Christian home should hear both — a father who will tell his children the truth about danger, and who will also lift up their heads with the promise of Christ’s return.
roots_summary: Old English héafod (head) + up → early-20th-c. warning heads up! → mid-century sports adj. heads-up → 1970s–80s noun a heads-up (advance notice).
